tools.name: ask_user_question
tools.description: Ask the user a concise question when you need confirmation, a choice, or missing information before proceeding. An answer item with empty selected and no custom means the user skipped that question: continue without it, do not ask it again, and do not treat the skip as permission.

questions.description: Questions to ask the user before continuing.

id.description: Stable id for this question; echoed in the answer.

question.description: The specific question to ask the user.

header.description: Optional short heading for the question, such as "Confirm" or "Choose Mode".

options.description: Optional choices to show the user. If you recommend one, put it first and append "(Recommended)" to that label.

description.description: One sentence explaining the tradeoff or impact.

multi_select.description: Whether the user may select more than one option. Defaults to false.

tools.name: bash
tools.description: Execute a bash command (`bash -c`) and return its stdout/stderr. Each call runs in a fresh shell; pass `workdir` instead of using `cd`. Managed `$DSH_*` variables expose current harness environment facts. Long output is truncated to its tail; the full output is saved to a file whose path is reported when available. Provide `description` before `command` in the arguments. Before any delete or move, verify that the resolved absolute target path is the intended one; never run it against a computed path you have not checked. An unset variable expands to an empty string, so guard variables in such paths with `${VAR:?}`. Commands may run under a file sandbox; a blocked file operation is reported as `[sandbox: file access denied under <mode> mode]`, a policy denial: do not retry another way.

description.description: Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice, 5-10 words (shown in the UI). Examples: "ls" → "List files in current directory"; "git status" → "Show working tree status"; "npm install" → "Install package dependencies".

timeoutMs.description: Timeout in milliseconds. The executor applies its configured default and cap; on expiry the command moves to the background as a job instead of being killed.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path is resolved against it.

run_in_background.description: Run in the background and return a job id immediately (collect with job_output, stop with job_kill). No timeout applies.

sandbox_permissions.description: The narrowest wider sandbox mode for a one-shot retry of the exact command the sandbox just denied; the retry asks the user for approval.

justification.description: Required with sandbox_permissions: one sentence for the user explaining why this exact command needs the wider access. Use the language of the user’s current request.

tools.description: Create a persisted goal that keeps this session working across automatic continuation rounds. Use it when the direct human request is a long-running objective, even if the user did not say "goal"; not for single-turn work.

objective.description: The concrete completion objective inferred from the direct human request.

max_goal_rounds.description: Optional positive safe-integer limit on automatic continuation rounds.

tools.description: Edit an existing UTF-8 text file by replacing literal text.

file_path.description: Path to edit, resolved by the filesystem backend. Provide `file_path` before `old_string` and `new_string` in the arguments.

new_string.description: Literal replacement text. Use an empty string to delete the match.

replace_all.description: Replace all matches. Defaults to false; when false, old_string must appear exactly once.

sandbox_permissions.description: The narrowest wider sandbox mode for a one-shot retry of the exact operation the sandbox just denied; the retry asks the user for approval.

justification.description: Required with sandbox_permissions: one sentence for the user explaining why this exact file operation needs the wider access. Use the language of the user’s current request.

A TZID rule keeps local clock time across daylight-saving changes; generated nonexistent local times are skipped, and repeated ones occur once, at the earlier instant. DTSTART may be in the past; delivery starts with the first occurrence after creation. A one-time delivery is RRULE:FREQ=DAILY;COUNT=1. No SECONDLY; BYSECOND takes one value. COUNT is at most 1000; use UNTIL for longer rules. MINUTELY and HOURLY accept no BY parts, so select clock times with DAILY or WEEKLY plus BYHOUR and BYMINUTE. BYMONTHDAY and ordinal BYDAY require MONTHLY or YEARLY; BYYEARDAY and BYWEEKNO require YEARLY. Ordinal BYDAY cannot combine with BYWEEKNO. Each FREQ period allows at most 10080 candidates before BYSETPOS, which accepts at most 31 values. UNTIL is a UTC instant ending in Z. A TZID rule keeps local clock time across daylight-saving changes; generated nonexistent local times are skipped, and repeated ones occur once, at the earlier instant. DTSTART may be in the past; delivery starts with the first occurrence after creation. A one-time delivery is RRULE:FREQ=DAILY;COUNT=1. No SECONDLY; BYSECOND takes one value. COUNT is at most 1000; use UNTIL for longer rules. MINUTELY and HOURLY accept no BY parts, so select clock times with DAILY or WEEKLY plus BYHOUR and BYMINUTE. BYMONTHDAY and ordinal BYDAY require MONTHLY or YEARLY; BYYEARDAY and BYWEEKNO require YEARLY. Ordinal BYDAY cannot combine with BYWEEKNO. Each FREQ period allows at most 10080 candidates before BYSETPOS, which accepts at most 31 values. UNTIL is a UTC instant ending in Z. Script-body hooks:
- `agent(prompt, opts?): Promise<any>` — run one subagent to completion. Without `opts.schema` it resolves to the child's final text; with `opts.schema` (an object-rooted JSON Schema using ONLY type/properties/required/additionalProperties/items/enum/const/oneOf) it resolves to the validated object. Resolves `null` when the child fails (filter with `.filter(Boolean)`). Other opts: `label` (display), `phase` (progress group), and independent `provider`/`model` LLM target overrides.
- `pipeline(items, ...stages): Promise<any[]>` — run each item through the stages independently with NO barrier between stages (prefer this for multi-stage work). Each stage receives `(prev, item, index)`. A stage throw drops that ITEM to `null` and skips its remaining stages.
- `parallel(thunks): Promise<any[]>` — run zero-argument functions concurrently and await ALL of them (a barrier; use only when a stage genuinely needs every prior result together). A throwing thunk resolves to `null`.
- `phase(title)` — start a progress phase; `log(message)` — narrate progress; `args` — the tool call's `args` input, verbatim.

## README

# Durable Subagents for pi

**Subagents that never lose work, and never do it twice.**

Streams drop. Requests time out. Models return nothing. You quit pi. Your laptop reboots. Durable Subagents keeps going: it picks every subagent up where it stopped, in the same session. Every request is decided once and every step is finished at most once (what a tool did to the outside world before a crash is the one thing it cannot undo; see [What we do not promise](#what-we-do-not-promise)).

```
$ npx pi-durable-subagents chaos
  killed host ×1 · dropped streams ×1 · empty replies ×6 · out-of-order steers ×1
  duplicate runs ........ 0
  lost results .......... 0
  restarted from scratch  0
  AC4 wakes / reminders . pass
  all 9 scenarios ....... pass
```

You can run this yourself, offline, in about 2 minutes. It runs a three-step writer → reviewer → integrator workflow through the real product (a real pi main session, the orchestrator, real subagent pi processes and a scripted model). It injects one fault per scenario, then checks the journals and sessions: nothing ran twice, nothing was lost, and nothing restarted from scratch.

## Install

```
pi install npm:pi-durable-subagents
# or straight from GitHub (no build step; runs the TypeScript sources)
pi install git:github.com/purboo/pi-durable-subagents
```

This needs pi 1.0.x and Node.js 22.19 or later, on Linux or macOS. It has been tested with pi 1.0.2 on Linux. The CI configuration covers Linux and macOS.

Windows is not supported: process tracking, file locks, command calls and the login service exist only for Linux and macOS. On Windows the extension disables itself when pi loads it, with one message, and registers no tool. Under Windows, run pi inside WSL.

The `pi-durable-subagents` command line (below) is optional. Run it without installing through `npx pi-durable-subagents …`, or install it once with `npm i -g pi-durable-subagents`. Use the global install if you want the optional login service (`install-service`): a service must not point into the npx cache, so `install-service` refuses to run from there.

## What happens when…

| Situation | What Durable Subagents does |
| --- | --- |
| The stream drops, or the model returns nothing | Continues the **same** session. Finished tool results are kept. |
| A step runs past its `timeoutMs` (even inside a silent tool) | Stops it cleanly as `timeout`. Only time spent working counts; waiting for you does not. |
| You quit pi (Ctrl+D, `/quit`, closing the terminal) while subagents run | That session's workflows pause: nothing more is spent, nothing is lost. When you come back, pi says so; `resume` (or `r` in the list) continues them in the same sessions. Set `"onQuit": "continue"` to let them run on instead. |
| pi crashes or is killed (`kill -9`) while subagents run | The work keeps running. When you come back, the session that started the work is told what needs you. |
| The machine or the orchestrator dies mid-run | The next pi you open resumes the work. Finished results are kept and nothing runs twice. The resumed subagent is told that processes its tools had started (background ones included) were stopped, so it checks them instead of waiting for them. |
| You steer a subagent while it is asking you a question | Your message reaches it, in order. Nothing is rejected or lost. |
| Two steers arrive out of order and the second replaces the first | Only the second one applies. |
| A step is refused, or a dependency fails | The workflow stops that branch cleanly. Nothing is retried in vain. |
| A provider's usage window runs out (`No available accounts`, usage limit, quota exceeded, a daily quota at 0) | Found at the second refusal in a row, while pi is still retrying. A call in a pool continues **in the same session** on the pool's next model (within pi's next retry or two); new calls skip that provider. After 15 minutes the next call that wants it tries it once; when it answers, new calls and new generations use it again. A call with a single model waits for it instead of failing. Billing errors (402, insufficient balance) still fail at once. |
| A gateway answers HTTP 200 with a quota notice ("your usage window is used up") | Matched against the provider's `exhaustedPatterns` (see [Configuration](#configuration)): the provider is avoided until its next probe, like a quota error, the message never becomes the result, and the call continues on the pool's next usable model. Without one the call fails with `model-unavailable:` and the matched text (clipped to 200 characters). |
| A pool does not resolve (it names itself, it is empty, or one of its entries is not a model) | That call fails at once with `model-unavailable: pool "<name>" does not resolve: <reason>`. It is a configuration error of the call, not of the orchestrator: other calls are unaffected. |
| Two subagents would write in the same worktree | Only one runs there at a time. A call that can write (its tools include `edit` or `write`, which pi's default tools do) holds its git worktree's writer lock from its launch until it ends, also while it waits for an answer. Another writer for that worktree waits in order, and status shows `waiting for writer lock: <root> held by <wid>/<key>`. `writer: false` (a call that does not write there), `isolation: "worktree"` and `"writerLock": "off"` opt out. |
| A subagent waits for an answer for a long time | It releases its model slot and memory, then resumes exactly once when you answer. A forwarded answer prevents planned hibernation. If an execution was stopped after consuming the answer, recovery continues the same session without another answer. The question survives orchestrator restarts (also forced ones) and crashes, including one that hits before the subagent released its slot. |
| A subagent's work ends (finished, stopped, or cut off) | Every process its tools started ends with that execution, also ones started with `nohup`, `setsid` or `&`: they carry the execution's tag (see the limit below). For work that must outlive its turn, the subagent can start a durable command call with `run --wake caller -- …` (below). A `hold` run directly by its tools is no exception: a forced restart stops it and its lease is released. |
| A subagent runs in a worktree you made (`isolation: "none"`, the default, with `cwd`) | Durable Subagents never creates, cleans, moves or deletes that directory or its branch, also not on `prune`; `prune` deletes only its own state and the worktrees it created for `isolation: "worktree"`. |

## Use it

The main agent gets one tool, `subagents`. You ask in plain language, and the agent calls it:

```
subagents({ action: "agents" })
subagents({ agent: "worker", task: "Fix the flaky lease test" })
subagents({ command: ["npm", "test"], cwd: "./repo", timeoutMs: 1800000 })
subagents({ tasks: [{ agent: "scout", task: "…" }, { agent: "reviewer", task: "…" }] })
subagents({ chain: [{ agent: "worker", task: "…" }, { agent: "reviewer", task: "Review: {previous}" }] })
subagents({ workflow: "./batch.js", args: { … }, usageBudget: { costUsd: 20 } })
subagents({ action: "send", to: "<wid>/<key>", kind: "steer", message: "Don't touch the tests yet" })
subagents({ action: "send", to: ["<wid>/a", "<wid>/b"], kind: "notify", message: "Config is TOML from now on" })
subagents({ action: "status" })
```

`status` without a wid is brief: what runs, what asks (with the address to answer) or failed, and one line per finished workflow, each with its run `labels` clipped to 60 characters (the `/subagents` list shows them on a workflow's row when they fit). A workflow's `status` is its run's result; `active: true` means a latest-generation call is still queued, running or asking, including a follow-up on a finished run. `status` with a wid shows one workflow with outputs clipped; add `key` for one call's full result, or `full: true` for everything. `tail: N` gives the last N lines of each call's result instead, and `grep: "<regex>"` only its lines matching a case-sensitive JavaScript regular expression (both: grep first, then the last N); either is unclipped up to 4000 characters per call, which suits a receipt on the last line of each output. An invalid regex is an error. The regex runs in the process that asks (the pi session or the CLI), so avoid nested quantifiers such as `(a+)+`, which can take seconds on one line; to bound its cost it tests only the first 2000 characters of a line and the last 5000 lines of an output (the reply then starts with `[n earlier lines not searched]`). When a run replies `{submitted: {rid}}` (its workflow was not created within 10 s), the rid works wherever a wid does. A call's `model` in `status` is the model its last provider request used; a requested switch not used yet shows as `switching`, a refused one as `switchFailed`. A send naming a model replies with `model` and `effect` (`next-request`, `next-execution` or `next-generation`). A provider's refusal of the content (terms of service, usage policy) fails the call at once with that error instead of retrying it. With `tasks` or `chain`, top-level `agent`, `model`, `timeoutMs`, `budget`, `isolation`, `context`, `tools`, `skills`, `once` and `writer` apply to every step that does not set its own, e.g. `{ tasks: [{ task: "…" }, { task: "…" }], agent: "reviewer" }`. A command step takes only `timeoutMs` and `writer` of them, plus `env` and `rerun`, which apply to command steps only (see [Command calls](#command-calls)). A top-level `task` or `command` beside a list is refused (each is a single call; put it in a step); other call fields there, and any of them beside a workflow script, are refused rather than ignored. When a call of a new run already waits for its worktree's writer lock as the run reply is written, the reply names it: `writerWait: ["<wid>/<key> held by <wid>/<key> (<root>)"]` with a hint that `writer: false` or `isolation: "worktree"` opts out. The reply does not wait for this.

Every run is asynchronous. The agent is woken once, when the workflow finishes (the notice carries each subagent's result) or when a subagent asks it something. Each verb means one thing, and a refusal says what would work:

| Verb | Applies to | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `run` | —   | Start one subagent, a command call, `tasks` in parallel, a `chain`, or a workflow script. An unknown agent name is refused before anything starts, with the list of agents. |
| `send steer` | a running subagent | Reaches it at its next safe point. To a finished one: refused, use `follow-up`; To one waiting on its question: it interrupts the question, and the subagent usually asks again; `answer` answers it. |
| `send notify` | any subagent | Tells it a decision without disturbing it. The reply's `delivery` says how: `steered` (running: it gets the note at its next safe point, like a steer), `held-until-answer` (waiting on its question: never interrupts it; it gets the note at the first safe point after the answer) or `noted` (not running: nothing starts; the note is recorded, and the call's next follow-up opens with it). |
| `send follow-up` | any subagent | A finished one continues in the same session as a new generation (`key@2`); the reply names it (`generation`, `call`). A running one gets it after its current turn; the reply says `delivery: forwarded` and names the running generation (`call: <wid>/<key>@<gen>`). With `model` (a model or a pool's name), the generation that takes it runs on it. |
| `send answer` | an open question | Answers it once, at the first chance: as the result of the question it waits on, or (when it no longer waits on that question, say after a steer) as a message at its next safe point. An answer to an earlier question while it waits on a later one ends the later one: that question is withdrawn (`superseded`, the subagent is told to ask again if it still needs it) and takes no answer. |
| `send model` | any subagent | A running one switches at its next request; one asking, hibernated or waiting for a slot launches on it when it runs again. A sealed one records a choice for its next follow-up, without starting anything or reserving a slot. An accepted manual choice persists across later generations until another manual choice replaces it (see [Model switching](#model-switching)). |
| `stop` | a subagent or a workflow | Final: `stopped`, usage kept, edits left as they are. A command call's whole process tree ends. |
| `drain` / `resume` | existing workflows | A reversible hold; runs started later are not held. |

Notes recorded for a call that is not running are durable and pending until its next follow-up, whose opening message carries all of them, in order, before its own message:

```
Notes recorded after your last turn:
- Config is TOML from now on
- Keep the old parser for one release

<the follow-up's message>
```

Each note is delivered once, also across orchestrator restarts and retried requests. A notify accepted for a running call that seals before it gets the note becomes a pending note too. `status` shows them on the call (`b@1 ok "..." · 2 notes pending`; JSON `notesPending`).

A follow-up queued into running work is not lost when that generation ends before taking it: the next generation opens with it, after any pending notes, as if it had been sent just after the end. A follow-up sent to the finished call in the meantime opens that generation and takes the queued ones along (in the order sent, before its own message). A retry of the same request then names the generation it went into. Only a stop drops it, because a stop is final; a withdrawn follow-up is gone too.

`to` may list several calls for `steer`, `notify`, `follow-up` and `model` (`answer` takes one). Each call gets its own request and is decided on its own: an unknown or refused target does not affect the others, and the reply has one entry per target (`targets`, plus a `summary` line each). With `request: "<id>"`, the target at position i (1-based, in the order given) is sent as `<id>:<i>`, so a retry with the same list gets the same outcomes and sends nothing twice. Each of those requests records the whole list, so another message, another list (longer, shorter or reordered) or a single send under that id is a `request-conflict`, and nothing of it is sent. The list is compared as written: retry with the same addresses (the same run id or `wid/key` form), or the retry is a conflict too.

`notify` is new in 1.0.28: after upgrading, restart the orchestrator (`pi-durable-subagents restart` or the tool's restart action) before using it. While an older orchestrator runs, a notify is refused with that advice and nothing is sent (an older orchestrator would accept it and drop it).

### Asking the parent

A child uses `ask` to ask its parent a question and wait for an answer or steering message. `{question: string}` still works by default. For a decision that the parent can act on, name the decision, options and evidence:

```
{
  "question": "The local repair is verified; should I keep this scope?",
  "decision_needed": "Choose the repair scope.",
  "options": [
    {"label": "Local fix", "scope": "ask projection", "cost": "one verification run", "risk": "low", "preferred": true},
    {"label": "Defer the repair"}
  ],
  "facts": ["commit 5ad9ee3", "run AK", "log sha abc"],
  "tried": ["reproduced the projection loss"],
  "classification_candidates": [
    {"label": "projection loss", "evidence": ["digest drops fields"], "unproven": ["restart path"]}
  ]
}
```

`question` is always required and must be a string. The optional fields are:

-   `decision_needed`: one sentence naming the decision you need; required and nonblank whenever any structured field is present.
-   `options`: at most 9 objects with required `label` and optional `scope`, `cost`, `risk` (strings) and `preferred` (boolean). At most one may be preferred; the parent sees numbered labels, with `(preferred)` on that one.
-   `facts` and `tried`: at most 20 strings each; give durable evidence (commit, run id, log sha) and what you have already tried.
-   `classification_candidates`: at most 9 objects with required `label` and optional `evidence` and `unproven` arrays of strings, separating evidence from explanations not yet proved. These nested arrays have no additional item-count limit.

Every string in a structured ask, including `question`, is at most 2000 characters. An ask is structured when any optional field above is present, or when `askRequireDecision` is true (see [Configuration](#configuration)). Default question-only asks keep the 1.1.0 behaviour, including no new question-length limit. Empty arrays are allowed; omitted fields stay absent, and text is preserved, not trimmed or coerced.

Wrong types, exceeded limits, multiple preferred options or a missing decision produce a tool error starting `ask refused:` before any question entry, attention item, waiter or revision is created. A missing decision says exactly:

```
ask refused: decision_needed is required (one sentence naming the decision you need), then options
```

The child can correct it and ask again. Parent-facing asking notices, the agent tool's status text, and CLI status/describe text show the decision first, then numbered option labels, then the original question. Plain questions still display as before. The supplied fields survive sessions, digests, attention and orchestrator restarts; question identity (`qid`, based on execution and question text), answer, steer and hibernation semantics are unchanged. JSON fields are described under [Driving dsa from a program](#driving-dsa-from-a-program).

### Model switching

In 1.2.0, an accepted manual `send kind:model` becomes the logical call's choice for every later follow-up generation (g+1, g+2, …), including calls initially launched from a pool. Another accepted manual model switch, or a follow-up specifying `model`, replaces it. Refused, withdrawn or replaced requests never become choices; automatic failover never becomes a choice.

A concrete `provider/id[:thinking]` remains concrete. A pool name remains a pool choice, resolved again at each generation's launch using the current pool configuration. Pool availability, slot, skip and failover rules still apply. A concrete choice follows the existing 1.1 explicit-model launch path: it has no pool to widen into, so an exhausted provider waits for availability/probing and provider slots, not an invented fallback pool. Live-switch capacity admission and reservations are unchanged.

To a sealed call, `send kind:model` records the choice and replies with `model` and `effect: "next-generation"`; it creates no generation, starts no child and reserves no slot. Send a follow-up to continue. Until then, `status` retains the last actual `model` and shows the pending choice as `switching`. Opening the next generation consumes the pending indicator, not the choice. Sealed model requests use the existing sealed follow-up acceptance path, including done and stopped workflows; address, stale-revision, command-call and pin-validation refusals still apply. This does not resume a stopped workflow by itself.

The choice is persisted before the applied reply and survives orchestrator restarts; a retry with the same request id returns the first outcome. Legacy model forwards without the new optional `choice` retain their 1.1 execution-only semantics; upgrading does not make an old switch sticky.

### The exact fork

`context: "exact"` runs a call as a continuation of the _calling_ pi session's last provider request: the parent capture supplies every field of that request byte for byte (system prompt or instructions, tools, tool choice, model, thinking, max tokens, prompt cache key, metadata), and the child's own conversation is appended to the parent's conversation. The child's agent definition, context files and skills never reach the provider. This is the third context value next to `"fresh"` (a call with no context of its own) and `"fork"` (a call that inherits the parent's effective context as pi sends it): the fork copies the parent's _messages_, the exact fork copies the parent's _whole request_ and adds the child's turns to it.

The parent session is the one that starts the call. It writes its latest provider payload to `$DSA_HOME/exact/<sessionId>.json` (mode 0600, atomic replace, off the request path); the file holds the serialized provider payload and the request's identity (the session id, provider, model, api, thinking and the time of the request), never headers and never credentials. The orchestrator removes capture files that were not modified for 7 days when it starts. `"exactCapture": false` turns the capture off: no file is written and an exact run falls back (`no-capture`).

A run whose specs are known (the call, `tasks`, `chain`) takes its context from that spec. A workflow script's specs are built while it runs, so there the run is admitted as an exact run only when its source names `"exact"` (or has `"exact"` as one of its `args`), and it needs an origin session like any other exact run. A call's own spec keeps its `context` in every form, a script's `runs.run` spec included.

An exact run pins the capture of its origin session at admission, so a later capture never changes a pinned run, and a follow-up of the call reuses it. The call launches on the captured provider, model and thinking: it holds that provider's slot and waits for it like any launch, and it has no pool failover (a provider that is used up makes the call fail as a concrete model would).

Two things are refused at admission: a call with `context: "exact"` that also names a `model` (`context "exact" runs on the origin model; remove model`), and an exact run without an origin session (`context "exact" needs an origin session: run it from a pi session, or give --origin-session <pi session id>`). From the CLI, `--origin-session <pi session id>` names that session; it is accepted only for `context: "exact"` calls.

The tools the model sees are the parent's. The call's own tools (the spec's tools or the agent's, plus the protocol tools) are the allow-list, enforced when the model calls a tool: a tool outside the allow-list, a tool the capture lists but the exact child cannot execute, and always `subagents` (no recursion) are refused with a result starting `tool refused in exact fork:`, and the child continues. A request on another provider, model or api than the capture is not sent: the call fails with `exact-mismatch: <detail>`. Anthropic cache breakpoints of the parent's conversation are kept; the child's own markers are kept only while the request stays within the provider's limit of four, the child's earliest one first.

A call that cannot be exact at launch runs as `context: "fork"` and records why:

| reason | when |
| --- | --- |
| `no-capture` | the origin session has no capture (the capture is off, or the session made no request yet) |
| `api:<name>` | the capture's api cannot be spliced (only `anthropic-messages` and `openai-responses` can) |
| `model-unknown` | the captured provider is not configured for the orchestrator |
| `no-payload-hook` | the child transport never offers the payload hook (detected at the first request) |

The decision is taken once per call: a rebuilt call never retries exact later.

`describe` of such a call adds an `exact` field (the mode, the reason of a rebuilt call, the pinned capture's sha256, size and time, the provider and model, the age of the capture at the launch, and the usage of every provider request). The status text and the finished-call notice show one line:

```
exact: cache 97% (148.2K/152.6K) · $0.031 · age 41s
exact: rebuilt (no-capture) · $0.031
```

The cache share is that of the first request (`cacheRead / (input + cacheRead)`). A provider's cache window is a few minutes: an exact fork of a parent that has been idle for longer is exact but reads little cache, and the ratio shows it.

### Forked context

`context: "fork"` pins the parent's _effective_ context, the one pi itself sends to the model, rather than every message on the session branch.

On a compacted branch the fork pins the latest compaction (its summary, shown as pi presents it, plus its `systemMessage` when it has one), the entries kept from its `firstKeptEntryId` on, and every entry after it — exactly as pi's session-context builder selects them. Raw messages from before the compaction are not copied, and system messages inside the kept range are dropped, as pi drops them. On an uncompacted branch nothing changes from 1.2: the `message` and `model_change` entries of the branch are pinned byte for byte.

dsa's own `dsa-*` receipts are never pinned, on either kind of branch, and neither are the entries pi does not send to the model (thinking-level changes, labels, session info). The child keeps its own thinking level. The pin is taken at admission, as before: a compaction in the parent after admission does not change a pinned run, and a follow-up generation reuses the child's own session.

### Workflow scripts

A workflow is a plain script. These are the globals it can use:

| Global | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `runs.run(key, spec)` | Run one subagent |
| `runs.all([...])` | Run several |
| `emit(value)` | Report progress |
| `args` | The workflow's arguments |
| `runs.input(name)` | A declared input file |
| `now()` / `random()` | Logged, so the run can be replayed |

The script's `return` value is the workflow result. A workflow script is a single file: it cannot `import` or `require` other modules.

`spec` fields:

-   `agent`, `task`, `model` (`provider/id[:thinking]` or a pool name), `cwd`;
-   `timeoutMs` (active time), `output` (a relative path becomes an artifact);
-   `schema` (a structured `report`);
-   `gate` (a command, or `{command, output: "json", schema, timeoutMs}`);
-   `isolation: "worktree"`, `context: "fork"` or `context: "exact"`, `budget`;
-   `writer` (`false`: the call does not write in its cwd's worktree, so it does not take that worktree's writer lock; `true`: it does, whatever its tools).

A spec with `command` instead of `agent` and `task` is a [command call](#command-calls).

A workflow script's specs are built while it runs, so the run is admitted as an exact run only when its source names `"exact"` (or has `"exact"` as one of its `args`); such a run needs an origin session (see [The exact fork](#the-exact-fork)). A run whose specs are known — the call, `tasks`, `chain` — takes its context from that spec. A call's own spec keeps its `context` in every form, a script's `runs.run` spec included.

The result has `ok`, `status`, the full `output` text and the structured `data`.

A script is replayed after a crash. Finished calls are not run again, and a changed script is detected rather than silently mixed. Keep scripts deterministic: use `now()`/`random()`, not `Date`/`Math.random`.

### Command calls

A command call runs a command instead of an agent: no model, no provider slot, no tokens. It is a call like any other: it has a key and an address (`<wid>/<key>`), it can be a step of `tasks` or `chain` or a `runs.run` of a script, and when it ends it wakes the session that started it like any finished call. Use it for a long build, a test suite or a wait that should not keep an agent (and its slot) busy.

```
subagents({ command: ["npm", "test"], cwd: "./repo" })
subagents({ command: "make -j8 && ./bench > bench.txt", timeoutMs: 3600000, env: { CI: "1" } })
subagents({ chain: [{ command: ["npm", "test"] }, { agent: "worker", task: "Fix what failed:\n{previous}" }] })
```

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `command` | An array runs a program with those arguments, never shell syntax: its first element is looked up in the command's `PATH` (exit 127 when there is none), and a shell builtin is not run as a builtin (`["exit", "7"]` looks for a program named `exit`). A string runs through `/bin/sh -c`. |
| `cwd` | Its directory, resolved like an agent call's. |
| `timeoutMs` | Wall-clock time from its start, including time the orchestrator was down (see the result table). |
| `env` | Variables added to the environment (`DSA_*` names are reserved). |
| `rerun` | `true`: when the process vanished without an exit record (the machine restarted), start it once more instead of ending `unknown`. For idempotent commands. |
| `writer` | `true`: take its worktree's writer lock (default `false`). |
| `key` | Its key in `tasks`/`chain`, as for agent steps. |

Other call fields (`agent`, `task`, `model`, `tools`, `schema`, `gate`, …) are refused in a command call, and `env`/`rerun` in an agent call. stdin is empty; stdout and stderr go, interleaved, to `output.log` in the attempt's directory. The command sees the orchestrator's environment plus `env`, `DSA_CALL` (its call id), `DSA_EXEC` (its attempt) and `DSA_HOME`, so a `pi-durable-subagents` command inside it (`hold`, `run`, `send`) addresses the same home; it cannot force a restart. After merging `env`, the command's `PATH` is `env.PATH`, else the orchestrator's `PATH`, with `$DSA_HOME/bin` appended once as the last entry. Custom and inherited tools keep precedence, and the CLI shim is still found. Empty entries and earlier copies of the shim directory are removed; an explicitly empty PATH searches only that directory, not the current directory or system tools. Agent PATH is unchanged (the shim stays first).

| The command | Result |
| --- | --- |
| exits 0 | `ok` |
| exits with another status or is killed by a signal | `failed`, error `Command exited <status>` / `Command killed by <SIG>` |
| ends after its deadline (start + `timeoutMs`), or still runs then | `timeout`, error `Command timed out after <ms> ms` |
| is stopped (`stop`) | `stopped` |
| vanished without an exit record, no `rerun` | `unknown`, error `Command ended without an exit record` |

`data` is `{exitCode, signal, durationMs}` and `output` the last 16 KiB of `output.log`. Only `stop` controls a command call (it ends the whole process tree); `steer`, `follow-up`, `answer`, `model` and `notify` are refused with `command call: <kind> is not supported (stop it, or start a new call)`.

The deadline counts from the command's start, also while no orchestrator runs: a command that ended in time is `ok` (or `failed`) even when the orchestrator records it later, and one that ended after its deadline is `timeout` (with its exit in `data`) although nothing had to stop it.

A command outlives the orchestrator: a restart (also a forced one), an idle exit or a crash leaves it running, and the next orchestrator takes it over or records its result if it ended meanwhile. The restart busy list does not count it.

A subagent can start a command that must outlive its own turn, then end the turn instead of waiting in a tool:

```
pi-durable-subagents run --request build-42 --wake caller -- npm test
```

When the workflow ends, the caller gets a follow-up with its status, each call's status and duration, command exit code or signal when known, and an output tail. Its first line is:

```
Durable run build-42 (<wid>) that you started with --wake caller finished: done.
```

A sealed caller continues as a new generation; a running one gets the usual forwarded follow-up, reopened after its turn if it did not take it. Each workflow completion has one durable wake decision, reused after retries and crashes. The ordinary finished notice to the CLI origin is unchanged. Every derived agent system prompt includes this lifecycle reminder; the pinned agent definition is not changed.

A hold (`drain`, `stop-all`, a quit pi) prevents starting, never stops what started. A command call that has not started yet (also one waiting for its worktree's writer lock) waits while its workflow is held and starts after `resume`. One that has started runs to its end; its result is recorded and delivered to its workflow as without the hold, also after an orchestrator restart (`start` and the pi session's starter start an orchestrator for it): a workflow that is then complete finishes and sends its notice, and a call it wants next waits for `resume`. The one `rerun` of a lost command is a new start, so under a hold it waits for `resume` too.

In a chain, a command step gets no `{previous}` (its command is not changed); an agent step after a command step gets the command's output as `{previous}`. `status`, `describe` and the `/subagents` view show a running command call with `command: <command>`, its pid and how long it runs instead of a model; `describe` also names its `output.log`. A finished one shows its status and exit code.

### Watch any subagent like the main agent

While subagents work, a small dock sits above the editor: one quiet row per working subagent (what it is doing and for how long; it spins while there is fresh activity and stops when the agent goes quiet), a question first and highlighted, and a summary line (`1 asking · 3 working · 12/40 done · ↓ subagents`). When the work ends it shrinks to one sentence and leaves after ten minutes. Set `"ui": { "dock": "line" }` (one line) or `"off"` in `~/.pi/durable-subagents/config.json`; `"ui": { "dockAt": "below" }` puts it below the editor instead. pi stacks the lines above the editor in extension load order, so to keep the dock above another extension's editor bar (a powerline bar, for example), list pi-durable-subagents before that extension in `packages`.

Press `↓` on an empty editor, or type `/subagents`, to open the list, a floating panel: this session's workflows (sessions are independent), working ones first (newest first), every subagent with its model, what it is doing and for how long, and its latest line. Finished ones follow, most recently ended first, dimmed, with their conclusion. A workflow's only subagent is named after the workflow (its `name`, else its label values, e.g. `nightly-qa c4811f14`); in a fan-out, a generated key (`tasks:0`) shows as its agent (`worker 1`, `reviewer`). The key remains the address for `send` and the CLI. A session's workflows include runs started through the CLI by a process this session launched (a background driver, a script run from its bash tool): pi exports `DSA_SESSION`, and `run` names that session (see `--session` below). Other sessions' and a terminal's runs are not shown.

A queued subagent says why it does not start, as far as the orchestrator has recorded it, and `queued` alone when nothing is known:

| phrase | meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `queued: orchestrator starting (12s)` | the orchestrator is still recovering workflows after a start; nothing is dispatched yet (`status` shows `orchestrator: <version> (pid N, starting 12s)`, the summary line `3 queued: orchestrator starting (12s)`) |
| `queued: <provider> usage window used up` | every provider it can start on is used up |
| `queued: waiting for the writer lock of <root>` | another call writes in the same worktree |
| `queued: waiting for a free slot (<provider> 4/4)` | every provider it can start on is full |
| `queued (answered)` / `queued (answered): <reason>` | an answered asker waiting to run again, with the reason when one is recorded (as above) |
| `paused · r resumes` | a drained workflow |

The CLI and the tool's status (`queued` per call) say the same.

The list is also where you act. The footer shows the keys for the selected row: `Enter` watch, `s` steer, `f` follow-up, `x` stop (asks `y` first), `m` model, `a` answer. A one-line input opens at the bottom (paste works), and the result shows right there: `✓ applied` or the reason it was not.

`Enter` opens a subagent full screen: its task, thinking, tool calls and output, rendered with pi's own components. `←`/`→` switch between the subagents of one workflow. Scrolling up pauses following; pi's `↓ Jump to latest message · End` badge (or `End`, or a click) brings you back.

Typing steers the subagent you are watching (`Alt+Enter` queues a follow-up instead), answers it if it is asking you something, and continues it (a follow-up) if it has finished. `/model` switches its model. Steers, answers and model switches are journaled as coming from you, and the main agent sees a note at its next turn.

### Quiet by design

The main agent is interrupted only when there is something to decide:

-   a question;
-   a finished workflow;
-   a stalled subagent (the alert names the command it is running and for how long, so a long silent command reads differently from a stuck call);
-   an unknown outcome;
-   a call waiting for another call's writer lock on its worktree (once, with the holder);
-   two unfinished calls observed editing the same worktree when one of them does not take the writer lock (a reminder);
-   a reached budget.

Each one arrives once. A reminder that was already resolved is shown as resolved, never as open.

Background checks stay quiet too. A slow round (a machine dozing in and out of sleep) is retried on the next one; a failure is shown once per streak as a pi notification, never written into the terminal under the editor.

### Activity for other extensions

A main session announces its subagent activity on `pi.events` whenever it changes, so another extension (a terminal-title spinner, a status bar) can tell that work goes on after the main agent settles:

```
pi.events.on("durable-subagents:activity", data => {
  const { sessionId, busy, working, asking, queued, paused } = data as {
```

Here's how the two shapes fit together, based on the [pi-durable-subagents package page](https://pi.dev/packages/pi-durable-subagents) and DSH's extension points.

## What pi-durable-subagents actually is, shape-wise

It's three things stacked:

1. **An orchestrator daemon** with a journal on disk (`DSA_HOME`) that survives crashes, `kill -9`, reboots, and the parent agent quitting. Every decision (run, send, answer) is recorded once; retried requests with the same `--request <id>` return the first outcome instead of doing the work twice.
2. **One tool (`subagents`)** given to the *pi* main agent, with verbs: `run` (one call, `tasks` parallel, `chain`, or a JS workflow script), `send` (`steer` / `notify` / `follow-up` / `answer` / `model`), `stop`, `status`.
3. **A CLI (`pi-durable-subagents`)** exposing the same operations as the tool, with `--json` everywhere, idempotent request-ids, and an event log (`events --all --since <cursor>`). The README explicitly documents "driving dsa from a program" — that's the seam DSH would use.

The crucial property: **durability lives outside any session**. Subagent state is an address (`<wid>/<key>`), not a live in-context child. A finished subagent continues *in the same session* as a new generation (`key@2`) via follow-up; notes delivered while it's not running are held durably until its next turn.

## Mapping to DSH's native concepts

| DSH today | pi-durable equivalent | Difference |
|---|---|---|
| `subagent` / `subagent_fork` | `run` (single call) | DSH children are context-mirrors that die with the session; pi-durable children are separate pi processes that outlive DSH entirely |
| `workflow` tool (JS script) | `runs.run`/`runs.all`/`emit` script | Nearly identical authoring shape; pi-durable scripts are *replayed* after crashes with once-only call semantics, budgets, gates |
| `bash run_in_background` + `job_output` | command calls (`command: [...]`) | pi-durable command calls outlive orchestrator restarts and can `--wake caller` on completion |
| `create_goal` (goal survives continuation rounds) | durable workflows | Goal persistence is *inside* DSH's loop; pi-durable is work persistence *external* to any harness |
| `ask_user_question` | `ask` (child → parent) | pi-durable's asks survive crashes and hibernate; but they sit in pi's world, so DSH must poll for them |

## Integration shapes, lightest to deepest

**Level 0 — no integration (works today).** DSH's agent drives the CLI through `bash`: `pi-durable-subagents run --request <stable-id> --spec - --json`, then `status <wid> --json` / `events --all --since <cursor>` each turn. The request-id idempotency is exactly what makes this safe — a tool result lost or a retried turn can't double-run work. Wrap a small **skill** teaching the verb model (this is textbook AXI: one CLI, JSON out, bounded outputs) and the DSH model can already treat a durable subagent as a persistent agent to talk to.

**Level 1 — a DSH bundle exposing tools.** A plugin (per the dsh-doc plugin-development flow) that shells to the CLI and exposes `durable_run`, `durable_send`, `durable_status`, following DSH tool-design guidance (bounded outputs, identifiers not log dumps). Optionally a Client slot panel that polls `status --json` and renders pi's "dock" equivalent — 1 asking · 3 working · 12/40 done — inside the DSH web GUI. This is the best fit-to-effort ratio: pi-durable is *not* an MCP server, but its CLI is a cleaner programmatic surface than most MCP servers.

**Level 2 — deeper choreography.** A DSH `create_goal` whose continuation rounds check the `events` cursor and answer open `ask`s (surfaced via `ask_user_question`), or a scheduled task polling for questions from long-lived workers. DSH becomes the "parent" in pi-durable's ask/answer protocol.

## The "persistent agent to talk to" shape

Concretely it would look like: DSH runs `worker` on a task, the DSH session ends, tomorrow a new DSH session calls `status`, sees `<wid>/worker@1 ok`, sends a follow-up — the same pi session continues with all its context. Meanwhile `notify` leaves durable notes for agents that aren't even running, and `ask` delivers structured decisions (options, evidence, preferred choice) that DSH can relay to you verbatim.

## Where the shapes grate

- **It's a pi-ecosystem island.** Subagents are pi agents (`scout`, `worker`, `reviewer`, or your own pi agent files) running on pi's configured providers and pools — not DSH agents, presets, or DSH's model routing. You'd maintain model config twice.
- **No exact fork from DSH.** `context: "exact"` byte-captures a *pi parent's* provider request. A DSH session can't be exact-forked; the best cross-harness context you get is `context: "fresh"` with the task text carrying everything (closer to plain `subagent` than `subagent_fork`).
- **No push channel.** DSH has no hook for an external process to interrupt it; every "the workflow finished / a subagent is asking" signal arrives only when the agent polls or when you use `--wake caller` pointing at something that can reach DSH.
- **Assumes git worktrees** for writer locks and isolation; a DSH session workspace works as plain `cwd` (`isolation: "none"`), but then coordination with DSH's own concurrent edits is on you.
- **Platform**: Linux/macOS only, Node 22.19+, pi 1.0.x installed alongside DSH.

**Bottom line:** pi-durable-subagents is best understood as an *out-of-harness durable execution layer*. DSH's native delegation is richer in shared context but ephemeral; pi-durable is context-poor but persistent and crash-safe. The natural fit is a thin DSH tool bundle (or even just a skill + `bash` today) over its idempotent JSON CLI, with DSH acting as the polling parent that steers, answers asks, and picks up results across sessions.

tools.name: ask_user_question
tools.description: Ask the user a concise question when you need confirmation, a choice, or missing information before proceeding. An answer item with empty selected and no custom means the user skipped that question: continue without it, do not ask it again, and do not treat the skip as permission.

questions.description: Questions to ask the user before continuing.

id.description: Stable id for this question; echoed in the answer.

question.description: The specific question to ask the user.

header.description: Optional short heading for the question, such as "Confirm" or "Choose Mode".

options.description: Optional choices to show the user. If you recommend one, put it first and append "(Recommended)" to that label.

description.description: One sentence explaining the tradeoff or impact.

multi_select.description: Whether the user may select more than one option. Defaults to false.

tools.name: bash
tools.description: Execute a bash command (`bash -c`) and return its stdout/stderr. Each call runs in a fresh shell; pass `workdir` instead of using `cd`. Managed `$DSH_*` variables expose current harness environment facts. Long output is truncated to its tail; the full output is saved to a file whose path is reported when available. Provide `description` before `command` in the arguments. Before any delete or move, verify that the resolved absolute target path is the intended one; never run it against a computed path you have not checked. An unset variable expands to an empty string, so guard variables in such paths with `${VAR:?}`. Commands may run under a file sandbox; a blocked file operation is reported as `[sandbox: file access denied under <mode> mode]`, a policy denial: do not retry another way.

description.description: Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice, 5-10 words (shown in the UI). Examples: "ls" → "List files in current directory"; "git status" → "Show working tree status"; "npm install" → "Install package dependencies".

timeoutMs.description: Timeout in milliseconds. The executor applies its configured default and cap; on expiry the command moves to the background as a job instead of being killed.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path is resolved against it.

run_in_background.description: Run in the background and return a job id immediately (collect with job_output, stop with job_kill). No timeout applies.

sandbox_permissions.description: The narrowest wider sandbox mode for a one-shot retry of the exact command the sandbox just denied; the retry asks the user for approval.

justification.description: Required with sandbox_permissions: one sentence for the user explaining why this exact command needs the wider access. Use the language of the user’s current request.

tools.name: create_goal
tools.description: Create a persisted goal that keeps this session working across automatic continuation rounds. Use it when the direct human request is a long-running objective, even if the user did not say "goal"; not for single-turn work.

objective.description: The concrete completion objective inferred from the direct human request.

max_goal_rounds.description: Optional positive safe-integer limit on automatic continuation rounds.

tools.name: edit
tools.description: Edit an existing UTF-8 text file by replacing literal text.

file_path.description: Path to edit, resolved by the filesystem backend. Provide `file_path` before `old_string` and `new_string` in the arguments.

new_string.description: Literal replacement text. Use an empty string to delete the match.

replace_all.description: Replace all matches. Defaults to false; when false, old_string must appear exactly once.

sandbox_permissions.description: The narrowest wider sandbox mode for a one-shot retry of the exact operation the sandbox just denied; the retry asks the user for approval.

justification.description: Required with sandbox_permissions: one sentence for the user explaining why this exact file operation needs the wider access. Use the language of the user’s current request.

tools.name: get_goal
tools.description: Read the current session goal, including the id and revision that update_goal requires.

tools.name: glob
tools.description: Find files, not directories, whose paths match a glob pattern, including hidden and ignored files. Returns up to 100 paths in modification-time order; a larger result keeps the first paths and reports where the complete list was saved.

pattern.description: Glob pattern to match file paths against (e.g. "**/*.ts", "src/**/*.test.js"). A pattern with no "/" matches the basename at any depth, so "*" and "*.ts" both search the whole tree; include a separator to anchor the depth.

path.description: Directory to search in. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path resolves against it.

tools.name: grep
tools.description: Search file contents with a ripgrep regular expression. Returns matching lines with line numbers, grouped by file. Returns up to 250 matches; a larger result reports where the complete match list was saved.

pattern.description: Regular expression to search for (ripgrep syntax).

path.description: File or directory to search. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path resolves against it.

include.description: One glob filter for which files to search (e.g. "*.ts", "*.{js,jsx}"). Not a list; negation is not supported.

tools.name: job_kill
tools.description: Request cancellation of a running background job.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

reason.description: Optional short reason, recorded in the log and forwarded to the job.

tools.name: job_list
tools.description: List your background jobs (running and finished) with their ids, kinds, and statuses.

tools.name: job_output
tools.description: Read a background job: output since the previous read for stream jobs, or the result of a finished final-output job.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

wait.description: Block until the job finishes or the timeout expires; a timed-out wait leaves the job running. Defaults to false.

timeout_ms.description: Max wait in milliseconds with wait: true. Defaults to and is capped by configuration.

tools.name: list_agents
tools.description: List your entire subagent tree: the root agent and all reachable continuable descendants, including yourself. Rows carry names, descriptions, and status. A descendant's name is its path from the root, such as reviewer/checker. You can message any other agent in the subagent tree. running means it is working; inactive means no turn is executing; it does not indicate task completion, success, or failure. corrupt, unsupported, or unavailable means this row's own descendants could not be read; the row itself is still a member you can message. While you remain active, you will be notified when a direct child finishes; there is no need to keep checking its status. Use send_message to continue the conversation.

tools.name: list_subagent_models
tools.description: Inspect the routes available for explicit subagent model selection. No arguments: authorized providers. `provider`: that provider's authorized models. `provider` + `model`: that model and its reasoning efforts. Query when choosing an explicit child route or reasoning effort. Omit optional fields rather than sending empty strings.

tools.name: load_workspace_dependencies
tools.description: Get absolute paths to bundled Python and library directories, plus bundled Python distribution versions. Node.js and pnpm paths are included when the payload provides them. Python includes numpy, pandas, python-docx, python-pptx, openpyxl, Pillow, lxml, and XlsxWriter. Use these libraries for Office files unless the user or workspace instructions select another environment. When Node.js and pnpm paths are returned, run pnpm with that Node executable and pnpm script path. This does not change PATH or package-manager settings.

tools.name: plugin_manager
tools.description: List plugins or bundles in the current profile, enable or disable them, install a bundle, or remove an installed bundle. Every action requires danger-full-access permission or approval for this call. Approval does not change the session permission mode. Changes affect every session in this profile. List first to obtain exact identifiers. Package installation can execute allowed build scripts. Live profiles apply changes immediately, including upgrades of installed packages; a change result that is not applied carries nextStep, which says what to do or tell the user. Unmet DSH version requirements (engines.dsh, else DSH peer dependencies) block installation and activation. Version exemptions risk crashes and data loss: warn the user and obtain explicit permission for the exact plugin and runtime versions before granting one.

target.description: Plugin entry id, bundle package name, or installation spec, according to action. For an Official catalog entry, pass list_bundles installTarget.spec to install_bundle.

enabled.description: Required for set operations; defaults to true for installation. For set_version_exemption, true grants and false revokes.

runtimeVersion.description: For set_version_exemption: exact DSH version from list_version_exemptions. Target must be the manifest package-name@version, not an alias or version range.

acceptRisk.description: For granting an exemption: true only after warning the user about possible crashes and data loss and receiving explicit permission for this exact plugin/runtime pair. General installation permission is not enough.

approvedBuilds.description: For install_bundle: pass names from pendingBuilds only after the user explicitly approves running their install scripts in the conversation. This grants persistent permission for this profile.

registry.description: For install_bundle: the npm registry URL asked first, when the user names one; otherwise the configured registry is asked, and its configured fallbacks while a registry is unreachable.

limit.description: List page size, from 1 to 100; defaults to 25.

tools.name: present
tools.description: Declare existing files as final deliverables for the user. Hosts may show presented files only after your turn ends, so call it once the files are final. If the user needs to review files earlier, such as before a tool call that waits for their answer, link them in your message instead. Use it when the user needs a separate file, especially Office documents, spreadsheets, and slide decks; prefer your final response when that suffices. The user opens the current files; their contents are not copied.

files.description: Usually the 1-2 most important deliverables; at most 4 per call.

path.description: Path of an existing regular file. Relative paths use the Session working directory.

description.description: Brief description for the user.

tools.name: read
tools.description: Read a UTF-8 text file and return line-numbered content.

file_path.description: Path to read, resolved by the filesystem backend.

offset.description: 1-based first line to return. Defaults to 1.

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to return. Defaults to 2000.

tools.name: read_image
tools.description: Read a PNG/JPEG/WebP/GIF file and return the image itself. Large images are downscaled automatically; do not install image libraries or create thumbnails to inspect an image.

file_path.description: Path to the image file, resolved by the filesystem backend.

tools.name: schedule_create
tools.description: Create a scheduled task. At each occurrence of rrule, prompt is delivered to the target session as a scheduled message from the user. The result includes the task id and the next occurrence as scheduledAt in UTC and scheduledAtLocal in the zone of rrule. After downtime, only the latest missed occurrence is delivered. Delivery can repeat after a crash.

title.description: Task name of at most 120 characters in the user's language: action plus object. Omit timing, status, ids, and bracketed suffixes.

rrule.description: Supported RFC 5545 subset: one DTSTART line, a newline, and one RRULE line. DTSTART ends in Z for UTC or carries TZID with an IANA time zone; a fixed offset such as UTC+5 is Etc/GMT-5, with the sign reversed. DTSTART must name an existing local time. A TZID rule keeps local clock time across daylight-saving changes; generated nonexistent local times are skipped, and repeated ones occur once, at the earlier instant. DTSTART may be in the past; delivery starts with the first occurrence after creation. A one-time delivery is RRULE:FREQ=DAILY;COUNT=1. No SECONDLY; BYSECOND takes one value. COUNT is at most 1000; use UNTIL for longer rules. MINUTELY and HOURLY accept no BY parts, so select clock times with DAILY or WEEKLY plus BYHOUR and BYMINUTE. BYMONTHDAY and ordinal BYDAY require MONTHLY or YEARLY; BYYEARDAY and BYWEEKNO require YEARLY. Ordinal BYDAY cannot combine with BYWEEKNO. Each FREQ period allows at most 10080 candidates before BYSETPOS, which accepts at most 31 values. UNTIL is a UTC instant ending in Z. Example: "DTSTART;TZID=Asia/Singapore:20260901T080000\nRRULE:FREQ=MONTHLY;BYDAY=MO,TU,WE,TH,FR;BYSETPOS=-1"

target.description: this_session delivers to this session; new_once delivers to the same new session every time, opened at the first delivery; new opens a different new session for every delivery. New sessions use this session's working directory and preset. With this_session or new_once, a delivery waits until the previous one finishes, and only the latest occurrence that passed meanwhile is delivered. Use this_session for reminders and for follow-ups to this conversation; use new_once or new for independent work, such as a recurring report, and whenever the user asks for a new conversation.

tools.name: schedule_edit
tools.description: Update, pause, resume, or delete one scheduled task by id. Deleting does not retract queued messages.

action.description: update applies the provided fields, at least one; delete removes the task.

title.description: Task name of at most 120 characters in the user's language: action plus object. Omit timing, status, ids, and bracketed suffixes.

prompt.description: New instruction delivered at each occurrence.

rrule.description: New recurrence in the schedule_create rrule format.

target.description: Omit to retain the destination and its creation settings. Providing target replaces them; new_once reserves a different Session. New targets capture this Session's working directory and preset. Choices are the same as schedule_create.

active.description: false pauses the task; true resumes only if its timing has a future occurrence. Otherwise provide a new rrule.

expectedUpdatedAt.description: updatedAt from the latest result that returned this task; if the task changed after that result, the result is schedule_conflict and nothing changes.

tools.name: schedule_list
tools.description: List scheduled tasks, including tasks created from other sessions. Active tasks come first, ordered by scheduledAt.

active.description: true for active tasks only; false for paused and ended tasks only; omitted for all tasks.

limit.description: Page size from 1 to 500; defaults to 100.

offset.description: Number of tasks to skip; defaults to 0.

tools.name: schedule_view
tools.description: View one scheduled task by id.

tools.name: send_message
tools.description: Send a message to an agent. A working agent receives it at its next step; an idle agent starts a new turn with it. Returns delivery confirmation.

agent.description: The name of another agent in your subagent tree, as shown by list_agents.

message.description: The message to deliver to the agent.

tools.name: skill
tools.description: Load the full instructions for a skill. Call it before acting on a task that names or clearly matches a skill in the session skill catalog.

name.description: The exact skill name from the available skills list.

tools.name: subagent
tools.description: Delegate a self-contained task to a subagent (a separate agent that works in its own context) to offload focused, independent work — research, a scoped implementation, an analysis — so it does not consume this conversation's context. The subagent returns its result, not its intermediate steps. This tool starts an independently managed subagent and immediately returns its name. If you are still online when it finishes, the runtime automatically delivers its completion notice. The notice includes the final answer unless the child sent you a message just before finishing. Use `send_message` to steer it while running or continue its conversation after it finishes. Omit `provider`, `model`, and `reasoning_effort` to use child defaults, falling back to compatible parent values.

cwd.description: Initial child working directory. Relative paths use your current directory; omitted inherits it. Later directory changes in either agent are independent.

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the delegated task, for display. Use the language of the user's current request.

name.description: Optional short name for the subagent, unique among the subagents you create: lower-case letters, digits, and hyphens, starting with a letter, at most 32 characters; lead is reserved for the root agent. Omitted names default to agent-1, agent-2, and so on.

prompt.description: The complete, self-contained task for the subagent. It does not share this conversation's context, so include everything it needs.

model.description: Model id within that provider; requires `provider`.

reasoning_effort.description: Reasoning effort id; requires `provider` and `model`. Omit to use the selected model's default, even when it matches the parent or configured route.

tools.name: subagent_fork
tools.description: Delegate a task to a subagent that inherits this conversation: a child agent seeded with all completed turns so far (it does not see the current in-flight turn). Use this when the subtask builds on this conversation's context — a follow-up analysis, a review, a continuation — without consuming this conversation's context for the work itself. You receive its result, not its intermediate steps. This tool starts an independently managed subagent and immediately returns its name. If you are still online when it finishes, the runtime automatically delivers its completion notice. The notice includes the final answer unless the child sent you a message just before finishing. Use `send_message` to steer it while running or continue its conversation after it finishes.

cwd.description: Initial child working directory. Relative paths use your current directory; omitted inherits it. Later directory changes in either agent are independent.

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the delegated task, for display. Use the language of the user's current request.

name.description: Optional short name for the subagent, unique among the subagents you create: lower-case letters, digits, and hyphens, starting with a letter, at most 32 characters; lead is reserved for the root agent. Omitted names default to agent-1, agent-2, and so on.

prompt.description: The task for the subagent. It already sees this conversation's completed turns, so build on them freely and state only what is new.

tools.name: todo_write
tools.description: Record and update a task list to plan multi-step work and show progress; skip it for trivial single-step tasks. Add one todo per concrete step before you start. While work remains, keep the todos being worked on `in_progress`, several only when work runs in parallel. Mark each todo `completed` as soon as it is done.

todos.description: The COMPLETE task list, replacing any previous list.

content.description: What the task is — a short imperative line.

tools.name: update_goal

revision.description: Exact positive revision returned by get_goal.

Use this for work that fans out across many independent pieces — an audit over many files, a migration, multi-angle research, adversarial verification of findings — where you write the orchestration as a script instead of delegating turn by turn.

Script-body hooks:
- `agent(prompt, opts?): Promise<any>` — run one subagent to completion. Without `opts.schema` it resolves to the child's final text; with `opts.schema` (an object-rooted JSON Schema using ONLY type/properties/required/additionalProperties/items/enum/const/oneOf) it resolves to the validated object.
